key_insight: A prescribed-kinematics Resistive Immersed Surface (RIS) model can reproduce the main hemodynamic behavior of aortic valve flow nearly as well as a fully coupled Immersed Boundary (IB) model, but at much lower cost.
engineering_relevance: This suggests RIS is a practical option for valve-flow studies when realistic leaflet motion is available and full fluid-structure coupling is not necessary.
method: RIS: prescribed leaflet kinematics embedded in the fluid with a penalty force to match fluid velocity to leaflet velocity.
IB: fully coupled two-way fluid-structure interaction with elastic leaflets resolved in the flow.
Comparison on trileaflet and bicuspid aortic valve simulations using SimVascular svMultiPhysics and IBAMR.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that RIS predicts the mean transvalvular pressure gradient within 15% of IB, improving to within 5% when inlet boundary conditions are matched, while reducing computational cost by about 60%.
watch_item: RIS depends on having representative prescribed leaflet kinematics, so accuracy may degrade if the motion or inlet conditions are not well matched.
paper_title: Comparative analysis of resistive immersed surface and immersed boundary methods for aortic valve simulation
